item.title: He Made $300K from Videos People Fall Asleep To: Inside Youtube's AI Slop Economy
item.author: Sid Wudraq
item.content:encoded: Over the three years I've been doing YouTube, I've made somewhere around $250,000–300,000This is , a young man in a white T-shirt with a YouTube logo. He lives in a mid-sized European country and is building his YouTube business there. The average salary where he lives is $700 before taxes.He doesn't make podcasts or record tutorials. His superpower is AI content that you watch to fall asleep or while cleaning your apartment. And videos like these now account for around a third of the entire YouTube feed. Let's take a look at how the world of faceless channels works and who can make decent money in this business.«You used to be able to make a video with a single image and get paid for it» has been doing YouTube for four years and has been making money on the platform for three. His business model is simple: he runs several channels with AI-generated content. Some of them become popular, and he receives substantial payouts from YouTube.The platform obviously doesn't mind getting extra views and making extra money. After all, when a creator makes a dollar, the platform makes two. YouTube isn't against artificial intelligence; it's against abuse. They want to minimize the number of ‘creators’ sitting 20 people in a basement and churning out these videosHe says that in the past, you could make a video with a single image and get it monetized. That approach no longer works., another experienced YouTube:One person used to be able to run dozens of channels with low-quality content. Today, thanks to AI and automation, you can launch hundreds of channels, although there isn't enough audience for all of them. That's why YouTube is gradually tightening its requirements. Problems arise when a creator simply publishes videos without adding anything of their own.Another creator, , lives in India and has been working with YouTube for several years. Based on his experience, YouTube as a platform generally has no problem with AI-generated content. Problems start when very low-quality videos are published:AI has made content creation easier, but it has also made competition on YouTube extremely high. Everyone has access to the same tools, but there is a difference in how they use them. It's important not to rely on them entirely, but to develop your own creativity as well. At the very least, edit the videos yourselfYouTube's rules do not prohibit running multiple channels from a single account, but if even one of the channels violates YouTube's rules, all the other connected ones will also be blocked. As AI channels began to grow rapidly, YouTube's opaque rules prompted creators to turn to specialized services that allow them to create channel networks without risking the complete loss of their business if they get banned., Head of Marketing at Octo Browser:We noticed a large number of users making money on YouTube starting around autumn 2025. At that time, the number of our users from India, Bangladesh, and Eastern Europe grew noticeably. Based on feedback from our users, most of them work on 2–3 channels simultaneously, but some have as many as 100. During interviews, YouTube creators often complained that platform bans were difficult to predict and the rules were not transparent. There are risky niches, such as anything related to children-oriented content. On top of that, YouTube doesn't clearly define the quality criteria for AI-generated content. Any violation can result in lost income. Because of this, creators have to use account separation methods with anti-detect browsers to work safely. With this approach, if one account gets banned, at least the others will continue workingHow many views do AI channels get?AI slop obviously emerged alongside generative AI, and it has now become a very important part of YouTube. According to a , this type of content currently accounts for 21–33% of all content on YouTube.It's easy to explain this volume. In the past, a creator had to spend a long time writing a script, shooting a video, or selecting footage. Now, all you need is a good prompt in Claude, a little magic in Nano Banana and ElevenLabs, and voilà—the video is ready in just 15 minutes.Despite how easy they are to produce, these videos attract very large audiences, comparable to those of top «traditional» YouTube channels.According to , the most-viewed AI channel is the Indian . In 2025, it received 2.07 billion views, and its estimated annual revenue is $4.25 million. The content depicts AI-generated scenes from the lives of ordinary Indians, with… realistic monkeys also taking part.The American Spanish-language channel Cuentos Facinantes has the most subscribers among slop channels worldwide: 9.73 million. They make AI-generated fairy tales for children.According to , most creators of AI content on YouTube are based in middle-income countries, such as Ukraine. There are also many of them in India, Pakistan, Nigeria, and Kenya. For them, this is an opportunity to earn money far exceeding the average salary in their countries.At the same time, Alex, an Eastern European content creator, says there are probably many such creators in the US as well, but they make completely different videos on different topics.How much can you make from AI slop?YouTube offers two levels of monetization.The first requires 500 subscribers, at least 3 public videos within 90 days, and one of the following: 3,000 hours of watch time on regular videos over 365 days or 3 million Shorts views over 90 days.The second level requires 1,000 subscribers and one of the following: 4,000 hours of watch time on regular videos over 365 days or 10 million Shorts views over 90 days. It provides broader access to the YouTube Partner Program.But in February 2027, YouTube plans to tighten its monetization rules and significantly raise the threshold.YouTube ad revenue is usually calculated using RPM—revenue per 1,000 views. estimates that one million views on long-form videos can generate $5,000–12,000, while one million Shorts views brings creators $50–200.RPM varies greatly by niche. According to publicly available data from large faceless channels, history videos focused on the US can generate $7–14 per 1,000 views, while true crime can generate $6–12 per thousand. Mythology and folklore bring in $5–9, popular science and explainer videos $6–11, personal finance $10–25, and tech reviews $8–15.Besides direct YouTube monetization, creators have other ways to make money. They can run livestreams, add sponsorships, create branded integrations through YouTube Studio, or tag products directly in videos.Regular commercial sponsors also reach out, but according to , these offers aren't particularly lucrative.I often get various collaboration offers by email. For example, they ask me to put a link in the video description, add an integration at the beginning of the video, send traffic to an affiliate website, and so on. But these offers are nowhere near comparable to monetization revenue, especially when it comes to English-language content. For example, a channel might make around $500 a day, while they offer $150 for a month-long collaboration.There are also creators who make money through channels other than AdSense. , for example, says he actively diversifies his income. He has sponsored integrations from software and AI companies that want to reach his audience. Another part of his income comes from affiliate marketing. He leaves links to products that are useful to his audience and receives a commission when someone makes a purchase:I think this is one of the main advantages of building an audience on YouTube. When you have a relevant audience, you're no longer dependent solely on monetization. You can build multiple income streams: sponsorships, affiliate programs, digital products, courses, or other services. Personally, I believe it's better to develop several income streams than to depend entirely on YouTube ad revenue.Who can make good money on YouTube?If you're starting a career as a YouTuber, remember this: it's not easy money, it's a profession just like any other. Having a good eye for content is important. That's why you have to watch hours and hours of the same kind of AI slop and figure out why a particular video got so many views.Discipline and perseverance are important. Many people don't want to sit at a computer for many hours a day, but that's what it takes. You often have to work a lot without seeing any results. You can make twenty videos and only the twenty-first one takes off.At the same time, technical skills are becoming less important. AI has greatly simplified the process, and modern editing programs such as CapCut are genuinely not difficult to learn.It's very important to learn how to work with AI properly. It's your catalyst: the faster you can create videos with it, the higher your productivity.The basic stack for a beginner YouTuber looks like this:ElevenLabs for generating voiceoversClaude for writing scripts and copyNano Banana, ChatGPT for generating imagesWhat kind of content performs well? YouTuber divides it into two types:Trending content, where you need to know what’s happening right now and understand which characters or events generate trafficEvergreen content, which can consistently attract good viewsSome say: find a niche you like and it will make you money. But that's not true. You need to find a niche that makes money. And make money from it so you can do things you enjoyNiches that are currently popular include:Everything related to GTA VI.News. The advantage of this niche is that you don't have to think about content because something is always happening. But don't resort to sensationalism or make things up.Personal finance: how to save money, what the price of gold or silver will be.Historical content: the history of Egypt in 20 minutes, Byzantium, excavated pyramids, sensational discoveries in the Amazon jungle. People love watching this kind of content.If you're just starting out on YouTube, choose a language whose cultural context you understand best. Don't chase English just because it has the highest monetization; competition is enormous there.Psychology videos in Czech performed very well for us. It's not the poorest country, and competition is very low. A video could bring in $1,000A lot of info-business entrepreneurs have appeared on the platform, and people often assume that YouTube is an easy way to make money. People see a distorted picture on social media and think everything will be easy. It seems that 90% of people come in with these expectations.Don't spread yourself too thin, and listen less to those who promise quick results. First, understand how YouTube works, what the platform looks like, and how its algorithms and monetization work. Then focus on content quality, and only after that on revenue.Money matters, and most people come to YouTube precisely because of it. But if you focus on making money too early, it will hinder your development. At the start, it's important to stay calm and learn the platform step by step.

item.title: I Can’t Believe A Silly Star Wars Racing Roguelite Is One Of My Favorite Games This Year
item.author: Jordan Ramée
item.content:encoded: I felt such a sense of whiplash jumping into Star Wars Galactic Racer after playing Zero Company. Unlike Zero Company--and plenty of the other Star Wars games we've gotten in recent years, like Survivor and Squadrons--Galactic Racer isn't trying to emulate the science-fantasy drama that defines the majority of the Star Wars movies and other assorted fiction. Instead, it's silly. We're not making morally gray decisions in a fight against an evil empire here. No, we're trying to win a racing league in order to dethrone the comically evil rich competitor mounting some kind of hostile takeover of the league. Oh, and we have an infinite number of chances to qualify, and protagonist Shade can walk away from the most violent of wrecks without a scratch. It's such a ludicrous situation that makes no sense if you think through the logistics of it for even a moment. And yet that very absurdity is exactly what racing in the Star Wars universe is all about. It sees competitors strapping themselves into barely functioning death machines to jockey against each other at breakneck speeds while soaring past lava, through narrow desert canyons, over acid-filled valleys, and alongside icy cliffs to the cheers and jeers of a bloodthirsty audience. Everything about the competition is comically ridiculous, and by leaning into that irrationality, Galactic Racer not only feels authentic to that fantasy, but it's also a hilariously good time. You race through the game as Shade, a former-racer-turned-cargo-pilot, who finds themselves brought back into the sport as both a favor to the league's commissioner and as a means of seeking revenge against Kestar Bool, an arrogant champion who wronged Shade in the past. Galactic Racer doesn't do too much to set up the stakes for this plot, framing Shade's revenge through a lens of a mystery. What did Kestar do to Shade? Why does Shade always wear a helmet? Why is it so important for Shade to get Kestar to remember who they are beneath that helmet? Don't you want to learn these things? Yes, yes, I do.However, while the mystique surrounding Shade, their relationship to Kestar, and the ramifications of the racing league at large for the galaxy are all intriguing setups that drive much of the drama in the early hours of Galactic Racer's story, the payoff to these questions is disappointing. The story eventually tells us the answers, but they're often hand-waved off in brief conversations, while Shade and the rest of the cast barely show any emotion--the direction for the voice acting is pretty good, but the final result sounds a little stiff, and the character models barely move and don't seem to change expression at all. These shortcomings don't ruin the experience of playing Galactic Racer, but they do detract from any sort of emotional depth that might be provided by the story.The best part about the story is how it's framed. Galactic Racer's story is a roguelite, not a traditional single-player campaign. To face off against Kestar, Shade has to first qualify to participate in the racing league, and to qualify, they need to win qualifier matches across a number of different planets. If Shade is knocked out--by crashing one too many times or losing an important race, among other disqualifiers--they're forced to fly back to the starting planet of Jakku and attempt the run again. This is a fantastic gameplay loop for a racing game. While the order of the planets doesn't change (at least initially--more on that in a bit), the path Shade takes across each one is up to you. With every run, Galactic Racer randomizes two to three paths of progression, with each crossing into another at specific points to sometimes narrow down to only one way forward or ballooning out to multiple options. And each stop along the path is a different type of event. You might just be competing in a simple race, for example, or get asked by one of the other characters to help them test pilot a specially made vehicle through a trial. Some of my favorite events are Mystery Encounters, in which Shade meets up with a friend or foe to talk--the mystery is you don't know which until you've already chosen the event. In one, I saw Kestar demand Shade pay him back for a small fender bender, and when I had Shade refuse, I started the next race by immediately blowing up on the starting line, losing one of my do-overs, and Kestar gloating that I shouldn't have crossed him. It was so silly and surprising, I laughed out loud (don't worry; I rallied and went on to win anyway), but it's the example I think of now when describing how your chosen path can have unintended consequences. Most dangerous of all events are Eliminators, which slowly knock out the racers who are falling behind one-by-one--make it to the end and you'll earn extra rewards, but fail to keep up and you won't just lose the race; you'll be thrown back to the start at Jakku. The limited choices of what you can do next creates this thrilling sense of risk-versus-reward. Aiming for harder challenges can mean earning enough improvements to your speeder to finally win that final qualifier, a very tough race on all but the lowest difficulty, or it could be the one setback that sends you back to the start. There's a palpable tension to the campaign, enforcing the narrative stakes in a way that the dialogue between races never manages to. That tension carries into the moment-to-moment action as well. There's no guiding line in Galactic Racer, no voice in your ear telling you where to go or what to do, and no rewind function to correct a mistake. This puts the entire onus of individual decisions in your hands, and you have to make them at breakneck speeds because you go . Between the rumbling of your speeder through your controller, the escalating blurring of the environment, and the use of sound to emulate flying past objects, you feel like you're hurtling forward at speeds that should kill you, and it's only your quick thinking that can keep you from a multitude of career-ending crashes with every lap. This isn't a roguelite where you take stock of your options and make measured decisions; this is the slow accruement of muscle memory and honing of reflexes (and, heck, maybe mastering the Force) over repeated attempts to handle a rocket-propelled hover car. The design philosophy of each track leans into this idea too. While each planet offers its own unique challenges to deal with--Jakku's hot sun can more easily overheat your engines, for instance, while Sentinel I's pools of acid can melt away your speeder if you hover over them for too long--almost all of the tracks feature narrow tunnels, obtrusive obstacles, and exceptionally sharp turns. While there are a few outliers (Crait has an oval track in a wide-open salt field, for example), each track regularly pushes you into positions where you're jockeying against other racers for room and making quick judgement calls without a ton of space to maneuver. The tracks on some planets even encourage you to aim for the most narrow of routes. You can temporarily escape Jakku's burning sun in some places by avoiding the open fields of sand and speeding through the wreckage of a Star Destroyer, for example, and if you want to keep your engines from freezing on Ando Prime, you can thread the needle through the dastardly cramped heat lamps scattered about each track. These tight spaces make you feel like you're going even faster, as you need to regularly squeeze past obstacles in the blink of an eye to get ahead. Managing to do so is exhilarating, and forcing or tricking an opponent into succumbing to their own speed and crashing is even more so.Succeeding at events earns you more points to upgrade your vehicle's stats, like more powerful acceleration or tighter cornering, as well as cash to buy parts for your speeder for that particular run. I always loved purchasing parts that could maximize how much of a boost I could gain by drafting off opponents or increase how long I could "safely" push a speeder's limited but extremely powerful Ramjet into the red before it exploded and took me out with it--anything to get that extra speed. But I was never afraid to try something else and discover a brand-new favorite strategy. I'm sure plenty of tier lists will come out in the wake of Galactic Racer's release that will tell you exactly which parts you should purchase and which you're better off avoiding, but I don't think there's actually an entirely bad one. This game encourages you to experiment and doesn't punish you for trying something new or adopting a different kind of racing strategy. As long as you get to the end, that's all that matters.If you don't make it to the end, you lose all the upgrades and parts that you put into your speeder, but you can take all the points you accrued based on your performance in individual events to unlock stronger starting stats for your vehicle. You can also use these points to purchase other types of vehicles--you start off with only the well-balanced landspeeder, but the exceptionally fast speeder bike or quick-to-turn skim speeder might be more your speed. There's a separate pool of points for buying visual upgrades, none of which do anything beyond ensuring your ride looks how you want it to. It was tough for me to move away from my starting landspeeder after all the effort I put into customizing its aesthetic appearance and starting stats so that my speeder always began a run looking and handling just as I wanted, but Galactic Racer has a generous respec mechanic so trying out the other two (and falling in love with the skim speeder's knife edge mechanic) doesn't risk much beyond the time used to test them out.In addition, fulfilling specific requirements or proving your worth to other characters during a run can unlock more starting playstyles and favors for all future attempts. Playstyles let you determine what starting equipment you have, like better shielding to take hits or an ion blaster to stun opponents, while favors give you even more bonuses, such as starting a run with a do-over if you disqualify or earning extra money for making your rivals crash. Over 15 hours into Galactic Racer, I'm still unlocking something new with each run, and while this consistent sense of progression presumably cannot last forever, lasting this long has kept every run filled with excitement. It can be such a bummer to crash and burn just one or two events away from the final goal, but at least I know I'll have a bunch of cool new stuff to try out next time around.And man do I just want to keep going for that next time around. The framing of a racer within the looping nature of a roguelike is so deeply rewarding to keep playing through again and again.Ultimately qualifying for the race is merely Act 1 of the game's story. With each subsequent act, more planets are added, and the order in which you race across them changes. New types of tracks are added, as well as more environmental hazards like mines or storms or darkness. Sponsors start weighing in, asking you to complete challenges within a single run to curry favor and fortune, and a betting system lets you wager your cash that you'll beat a specific racer in a single event, allowing you to form brief rivalries for profit. As the amount of features and mechanics grow, the number of events you need to complete just to get to the next act keeps growing too. What starts as a simple roguelite racer where every run is 20-40 minutes eventually grows into a gauntlet where every skill you've honed is put to the test in a lengthy planet-hopping adventure that can go for well over an hour on just one run. You can't save your progress within a run either, beyond just letting the game idle and putting your console or PC into standby (which I often had to do because racing near-flawlessly for over 60 minutes straight is pretty brutal). Every mistake I made near the end of my final runs of the story filled me with a spike of dread, but reaching the end of a run and hitting a milestone in the plot always filled me with a rush of adrenaline and accomplishment. I still have yet to complete Galactic Racer's final challenge--I choked on the second-to-last event of the run and had to sit down to write this review so that I could calm down--but all I can think about is trying again.Granted, it's not all perfect. Galactic Racer has a good variety of tracks--enough to keep each run fresh as you try again and again, but few enough to let you slowly become familiar with them enough to develop strategies and discover shortcuts. But a few of the tracks, especially those on Jakku, have weird sign-posting that can make it irritatingly easy to get turned around and accidentally go the wrong way. And I can feel the lack of an excellent soundtrack as I continue to play. A few of the more recent Star Wars games have begun to dip into the culture of the galaxy far, far away--both Jedi games and Zero Company to an extent (and Outlaws)--and a big part of that has been getting to hear what in-universe music and radio stations sound like. So I'm baffled Galactic Racer doesn't give me anything to listen to while racing, save for the general ambient noise of each planet, a brief triumphant or defeated score to mark any of my victories or defeats, and the recycled shouts, quips, taunts, and proclamations made by the assortment of racers you hear whenever Shade passes them, gets passed by them, wins against them, or loses against them. Around hour eight or so, that repetition gets a little grating, and having something else to listen to might have alleviated that shortcoming.Playing Galactic Racer reminds me of my favorite parts of the most recent Forza Horizon games: the first 10 minutes. That initial drive sequence that introduces the new setting, gets you acclimated to the gameplay basics, and moves you from one track to another to let you play around with different vehicles in a bunch of different environments is so fun. It's all about hearing the roar of the crowd and the excitement in the announcer's voice, not needing to rely on the rewind mechanic, and just feeling the rush and exhilarating joy of going really, really fast in a cool vehicle as the world around you becomes a blur. Galactic Racer is those absolutely perfect 10 minutes expanded into a full game. Every moment feels joyfully fast. Every decision carries the weight of tension. And every run is a rewarding chance to learn, improve, tinker, and adapt, whether it ends in success or failure. I can't wait to keep playing what's been my favorite racing game in years.
